The domain is all natural numbers, but no restriction m>0 or explicit mod-zero convention is printed. At a=b=1,m=0, the positive-modulus meaning of congruence is undefined, whereas extending it to the divisibility equation would make a=b true. That extension is not supplied and is not adopted. Positive-domain algebra retained as audit evidence only: for m>0 and natural a,b, the formula $\exists u\exists v(a+mu=b+mv)$ is equivalent to m dividing a-b. A witness gives a-b=m(v-u); conversely write a-b=mt with integer t, take u=0,v=t if t≥0, and u=-t,v=0 if t<0, producing natural witnesses in both cases. Page 4 prints $\exists r\exists q_1\exists q_2(r<m\land ra=mq_1+r\land b=mq_2+r)$: its extra ra is independently wrong even for m>0, since a=1,b=3,m=5,r=3,q_1=q_2=0 satisfies it although 1 and 3 are not congruent modulo 5. Correcting that algebra cannot define the missing m=0 case. No verified Question is published.

Q-2025S-MID-P02-a-ii.label: 2(a)(ii)

At a=b=0, the greatest-positive-common-divisor definition gives an undefined term: every positive integer is a common divisor and there is no greatest one. Under a common extension gcd(0,0)=0, gcd(0,0)=1 would instead be false, but that convention is not adopted; undefined is not false. Page 4 prints $\forall k((\exists x\exists y(kx=a\land ky=b))\to k=1)$. Its a=b=0 instance is false using k=2,x=y=0, which cannot justify assigning a truth value to the undefined source predicate. Positive-domain algebra retained as audit evidence only: for a,b>0, any k with natural witnesses kx=a and ky=b must be a positive common divisor. If gcd(a,b)=1, every such k equals 1; conversely 1 always divides both inputs and the formula excludes every common divisor greater than 1, so their greatest common divisor is 1. This proves equivalence on positive inputs but does not settle the literal full domain. No verified Question is published.
